At the same time, we can imagine situations in which legal requirements make it unclear whether models trained on public data with uncertain origin are permissible, and where a practitioner is interested in retraining their language models using a specialized or trustworthy data source (Wilka et al. 2017; Gold & Latonero, 2017). In addition, we are motivated to benchmark the overall conceptual progress of research in this area over the last years, beyond simply turning the scaling knob. The goal of achieving BERT-like perfor- mance with modest training resources would have seemed unthinkable in 2018, and yet with modern advances and transformer training techniques this may now be possible. To answer these questions, we consider a challenge we call “Cramming” – learning a whole language model the day before the test. Our studies begin by investigating several facets of the training pipeline to see which modiﬁcations actually improve performance in the scaled-down scenario. We provide evidence that even in this constrained setting, performance closely follows scaling laws observed in large-equilibrium settings. We also conduct analyses to understand the extent of variation across different pruning methods, including batch-based and discrete pruning. Our results show that scaling down is hard; while smaller model architectures enable speeding up gradient computations, overall rates of model improvement over time remain nearly constant, with the exception of smaller models (Figure 1b). We also extend the scope of research to include quantizing all pruning parameters of a Transformer layer. In Figure 1c, we ﬁnd that even with these limitations, scaling down can yield improvements by enabling layer-wise transfer of interpolative bit-widths, such as int6 and int3. Finally, in Section 7, we also demonstrate that using a dense layer structure to represent model predictions results in improvements in several performance metrics, beyond just improving the base model's performance on the chosen task. Beyond improving chosen model pa- rameters, this approach allows for seamless extraction of necessary precision parameters from the training data. Over- all, the technique produces improvements over previous methods, pushing the boundaries of low-bit quantization for e!- cient LLM inference. 2.
